claims.text: The initial alloy is equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
The random solid-solution state has a BCC structure.
Atomic-size mismatch and random chemical distribution produce high lattice distortion in the random alloy.
Controlled annealing or Monte Carlo simulation can induce chemical short-range order in HfNbTaTiZr.
The induced SRO preferentially forms HfTi and TiZr binary clusters.
The binary SRO clusters undergo a percolative transition to B2-like ordered structures.
A continuous network of B2-like HfTi and TiZr clusters reduces local lattice-distortion amplitudes relative to the random state.
B2-like ordering reduces the variance of local atomic environments.
Reduced variance in local environments decreases the scattering cross-section for high-frequency phonons.
Percolating ordered clusters create coherent, low-resistance pathways for phonon transport.
Ordering increases the phonon mean free path.
Percolative B2-like ordering causes a net increase in lattice thermal conductivity relative to the random solid solution.
Ordering measurably modifies the high-frequency phonon density of states and is associated with higher phonon group velocities.
The ordered state has lower phonon scattering rates than the random state.
Atomic displacement amplitudes or Debye-Waller factors are lower in ordered regions than in the random state.
Random HfNbTaTiZr has low lattice thermal conductivity because lattice distortion and chemical disorder strongly scatter phonons.
The conductivity increase occurs only after the SRO clusters form a percolating network.
Isolated precipitates or phase separation decrease conductivity through interface scattering.
At sufficiently high temperature, anharmonic phonon scattering can dominate and suppress the proposed conductivity increase.
Significant porosity or oxide inclusions must be absent because they could dominate scattering and obscure the ordering effect.
